claude_take: Today's stories share a single thread: being big, rich or official no longer buys trust the way it used to. Nvidia's board cut Jensen Huang loose within days of a personal scandal breaking, no matter how indispensable he seemed to the entire AI industry's chip supply, and Stanford's own hundred-year AI study finds the public has had almost no real say in how deeply that same industry has already reshaped daily life. Richemont posted a better profit than anyone expected and got punished by the market anyway, the same instinct that let Johnny Depp's modest holiday comeback quietly beat a far pricier studio heist comedy at the box office. Meanwhile Chilean truckers are paralyzing their own country over a fuel policy set by decree, and a tech lobby is in a New York courtroom arguing it shouldn't even have to warn people about its own products, two very different fights over who actually gets a say, landing on the same day for a reason.
claude_take_title: Being Big Doesn't Buy Trust Anymore

items.headline: Nvidia's Jensen Huang Resigns as CEO Amid Espionage and Affair Scandal
items.summary: Nvidia's board accepted Jensen Huang's resignation after an independent probe into reports that one of his extramarital affairs involved a woman suspected of working for Chinese intelligence; CFO Colette Kress is now interim CEO while the board searches for a permanent successor, with Arm's Rene Haas reportedly among the candidates. The news briefly pushed Nvidia's market capitalization below $4 trillion and sparked a reinstatement petition with more than 100,000 signatures, underscoring just how central one executive had become to the entire AI industry's chip supply.

items.headline: Stanford's Third AI100 Report Finds AI Spreading Through Society Faster Than It's Paying Off
items.summary: Stanford's hundred-year study on artificial intelligence released its third five-year report, concluding that generative AI has moved from research curiosity to everyday infrastructure faster than almost anyone predicted. The panel of computer scientists, philosophers and sociologists found that AI investment is outpacing any previous technology boom without yet delivering matching returns, and that the public has had little real input into how the systems reshaping their lives were built.

items.headline: Johnny Depp's 'Ebenezer' Tops a Soft Weekend as 'How to Rob a Bank' Bombs
items.summary: Depp's modestly budgeted Christmas Carol riff 'Ebenezer' opened atop the North American box office, while Amazon MGM's star-driven heist comedy 'How to Rob a Bank' collapsed despite a far larger budget and a weak critical reception. The lopsided result extends a fall pattern in which cheaper, star-led comeback vehicles are quietly outperforming expensive studio bets, as 'Godzilla Minus Zero' also posted a steep second-weekend drop.

items.headline: Skydance's First Earnings Report as a Merged Studio Shows Warner Bros.' Slate Dragging on Profit
items.summary: In its first quarterly report since completing its roughly $81 billion acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery, Skydance executives said the legacy Warner film slate will cost the combined company about $200 million in adjusted earnings this quarter, even as Paramount's own titles outperform. The company is still targeting $6 billion in merger synergies within three years and a combined HBO Max-Paramount+ bundle in early 2027, but the results are an early sign of how bumpy folding two giant content libraries together will be.

items.headline: Tech Trade Group NetChoice Sues New York Over Social Media Warning-Label Law
items.summary: NetChoice, whose members include Meta, Google/YouTube and TikTok, filed suit in federal court in Manhattan to block New York's law requiring platforms with features like infinite scroll and algorithmic feeds to carry cigarette-style warnings before it takes effect on January 1, 2027. The case leans on a prior ruling that blocked a nearly identical Colorado law on First Amendment grounds, making New York the latest front in a growing legal fight between states trying to regulate 'addictive' feeds and an industry trying to stop them.

items.headline: Nationwide Truckers' Strike Paralyzes Chile Over Fuel Price Hikes
items.summary: Truckers and bus drivers across Chile launched an indefinite strike and highway blockades, disrupting ports, mines and salmon and fruit exports, in protest of fuel price increases that followed President Jose Antonio Kast's decision to alter the country's price-stabilization mechanism by decree. Kast has proposed capping weekly price rises, but talks broke down without agreement on the strikers' core demands, turning an economic dispute into one of the most serious early tests of his new hard-right government.

items.headline: Richemont Shares Slide Even as Cartier Owner's Profit Beats Forecasts
items.summary: Richemont's first-half net profit rose to €2.53 billion, above analyst expectations, and its jewellery division grew 14%, far outpacing luxury peers averaging low single digits, yet the stock fell as much as 9% on fears that growth is slowing. The shortfall came almost entirely from the Middle East, where regional sales reversed from 22% growth a year earlier to a 7% decline amid geopolitical tension, spooking investors about how durable the jewellery boom propping up the luxury sector really is.

items.headline: Study Finds Common ADHD Classroom Accommodations Don't Improve Student Outcomes
items.summary: A Florida International University-led trial published in JAMA Pediatrics gave 255 children with ADHD extra time, frequent breaks, standing desks and low-distraction workspaces, and found none of these common accommodations improved behavior or academic productivity, with some children doing worse. Behavioral interventions and stimulant medication, by contrast, did cut classroom rule violations substantially, suggesting schools may be leaning on the wrong tools to support ADHD students.

items.headline: Confucius's Ren (Benevolence)
items.summary: Ren is Confucius's term for genuine benevolence toward others, a virtue cultivated through proper relationships, ritual practice and honest self-reflection rather than through fixed rules handed down from outside. It still matters because it frames ethics as a matter of character and cultivated empathy, built gradually through everyday relationships, rather than abstract principles or laws, an idea that continues to shape debates over how virtue, education and social trust depend on one another.
items.summary_fr: Le Ren désigne chez Confucius la vertu de bienveillance authentique envers autrui, cultivée par la pratique de relations justes, des rites appropriés et une sincère introspection, plutôt que par des règles fixes imposées de l'extérieur. Cette idée reste pertinente aujourd'hui car elle conçoit l'éthique comme une question de caractère et d'empathie cultivée progressivement au fil des relations quotidiennes, plutôt que de principes abstraits ou de lois, une intuition qui continue d'éclairer les débats sur les liens entre vertu, éducation et confiance sociale.
